newsitem.title: UK: Road to EMU offers arbitrage scope in rate futures.
newsitem.headline: Road to EMU offers arbitrage scope in rate futures.

text.p: Derivatives markets currently discount lower interest rates in France than in Germany after European monetary union kicks off in 1999, an anomaly analysts say presents arbitrage opportunities for brave investors.
Economists are scratching their heads over post-1999 Pibor contracts trading at a notable premium over Euromarks.
But they agree there is money to be made out of the gap, since short term interest rates are set to converge under European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London, said it seemed a good idea to buy Euromark back-month contracts and sell Pibor, but there was a risk.
"If (EMU) doesn't go through, the spread might really hurt you," he said.
If EMU makes its debut as planned, on January 1 1999, short term rate convergence should mean contracts at the short end of the yield curve will be at parity for participating countries.
Economists say this makes the discrepancy in future prices unrealistic, and they admit being puzzled as to how it crept in.
"It's a very good question," said Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange, "because money markets would probably have similar or equal rates if monetary union goes ahead."
But he said it was not unusual for contracts so far in the future to appear ridiculous as the interest there was so small.

"You have to take into account that these contracts are not very liquid," said Mange. "If you take the open interest on the June 1999 contract it's tiny, and on the September and December contracts it's almost zero. The contracts are not traded, that's the problem - nobody looks at them."
Mange said this meant increases in trading on either contract could lead to big swings in price trends.
Some analysts said the premium could have arisen because the market expected French interest rates to ease in the EMU run-up.
"It depends strongly on what is assumed in terms of rates," said Mange, adding that the French economy had improved.
"I don't see any reason why short-term rates in France shouldn't go lower than in Germany," said arbitrageur Thierry Sebban at STAFF, a Paris futures brokerage.
French and German rates are already close. Germany's repo rate is at 3.00 percent and France's intervention rate is 3.10.

Expectations of a decrease in French rates could explain why the December 1999 Pibor future is trading at 94.89, 17 basis points over the December 1999 Euromark at 94.72. This compares to March 1997 Pibor at 96.69 versus the Euromark at 96.89.
Some analysts in London, however, were more inclined to put the anomaly down to the number of "Eurosceptics" in Britain and Germany.
"If (EMU) falls apart, France will cut rates drastically over Germany, which I think will still keep a very tight monetary policy," said Beauchamp.
He compared the market to 10-year bonds, where France is also at a premium, yielding 5.53 percent against Germany's 5.67.
"Why should the French 10-year be yielding 14 bps less that Germany? It's the same thing," he said. "I think it's purely showing an effect of what rates are in Germany and France now."
EMU aside, however, many analysts said the difference was largely down to players selling at the short end and buying the long end, after the French yield curve flattened out recently.
"It's not just a question of Pibor versus Euromark, it's more a question of short term versus long term," said Sebban.
"It's also a question of convergence," said Mange. "Whether the French contract converges to the German one or vice-versa."
